questions.title: Mean latency improved and the tail got worse
questions.prompt: Two changes shipped in one week: the target model moved to its next version, and a new customer whose traffic is mostly code was routed onto the same cluster. Speculative decoding has been on for months. Since then the mean inter-token latency fell 25 percent, the P99 rose 15 percent, and throughput at the usual concurrency is down. Diagnose it.
questions.short: Both changes attack acceptance. The draft head was trained against the previous target version, so its distribution drifted and more drafts reject; the code traffic shifts the input distribution away from the general chat data the head was trained on, where acceptance falls into the 0.4 to 0.6 band. A rejected draft costs a verify and a re-roll, two passes that serialize under a full batch, which is exactly a tail that worsens while the mean still improves. Read acceptance per traffic slice and per target version from the engine's speculative metrics, retrain or roll back to a head aligned with the new target, and gate speculation per request class.
questions.full:
### Why mean and tail move in opposite directions

Most requests still accept most drafts, so their inter-token latency falls and the mean improves. The requests that reject early pay the draft steps, the verify and a second target pass for the correction, and under a full batch those passes queue behind each other. The tail is where the rejected requests live. Watch P99, not P50.

### Cause one: a draft one version behind

A hidden-state draft is trained to predict a specific target's next token from that target's features. A new target version changes the features and the distribution, and the draft's agreement with it drops. The capstone's first exercise is to measure this degradation and to build the alert for it.

### Cause two: a domain the head never saw

A head trained on general chat sits at 0.6 to 0.8 acceptance there and at 0.4 to 0.6 on code, medical or legal traffic. Code tokens are predictable for a draft trained on code, and poorly predicted by one that was not. Below an acceptance of about 0.55 at high concurrency speculation is net negative, so the new customer may have pushed the cluster under the floor.

### The diagnosis

1. Pull accepted draft tokens and proposed draft tokens per request from the engine, divide the first by the second, and split by target version and by customer or request class. One number for the whole cluster hides both causes.
2. Compare the chat slice before and after the upgrade: if it fell, the version drift is real.
3. Compare the code slice against the chat slice at the same version: if it sits far lower, the domain shift is real.
4. Confirm the tail story by bucketing P99 by acceptance; the slow tail should be the low-acceptance slice.

### The fix

- Retrain the head against the new target version, or roll the target back until the aligned head is ready.
- Route the code customer to a plain decode pool, or train a code-specific head; the training job is light next to fine-tuning the target.
- Gate speculation per request class on measured acceptance, with an n-gram or draft-free fallback below the floor.
- Alert on acceptance per slice so the next version bump cannot ship without the draft.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why can the mean improve while throughput falls? Expected: the accepted requests get faster, but the rejected ones consume two target passes each, and at a full batch that extra work displaces other requests.
- **Level 4:** Design the alert in two sentences. Expected: compute acceptance per slice and per target version over a short window and compare against the baseline recorded at rollout; page when a slice crosses the floor or drops a fixed share from its baseline.
- **Level 4:** What is the fallback when acceptance drops on one slice only? Expected: switch that slice to an n-gram draft or to plain decoding while the head is retrained, and keep speculation where it still pays.
- **Level 4:** How does this change your release process? Expected: a target upgrade ships together with a draft trained against it, and the benchmark that gates the release reports acceptance and P99 per slice.
questions.wrong:
- "Increase the draft length to win back throughput." More drafts at low acceptance are mostly rejected and their cost is still paid; the tail gets worse.
- "Turn speculation off everywhere." The chat slice may still pay; gate by slice and fix the head.
- "The new target is just slower; speculation has nothing to do with it." A plain-decode benchmark of the new target settles that in minutes, and the mean improving while the tail worsens points at rejections.

questions.title: One step of byte-pair training and what it leaves behind
questions.prompt: Walk me through one training step of byte-pair encoding on a small corpus, and tell me what the trained artifact actually is.
questions.short: Start with every word split into base symbols, bytes or characters. Count every adjacent pair across the corpus, weighted by how often each word appears, merge the most frequent pair into one new symbol with the next free id, rewrite every occurrence, and repeat until the vocabulary reaches the target size. The artifact is the ordered list of merges; the vocabulary follows from it, and the same list applied in the same order is what encoding uses later.
questions.full:
### A worked step

Corpus: "lower" 5 times, "lowest" 2 times, "newest" 6 times.

```text
l o w e r      (x5)
l o w e s t    (x2)
n e w e s t    (x6)

pair counts: (w,e): 13   (e,s): 8   (s,t): 8   (l,o): 7   (o,w): 7   (n,e): 6   (e,r): 5
merge (w,e) -> we

l o we r       (x5)
l o we s t     (x2)
n e we s t     (x6)
```

Recount, and the next step sees (we,s) and (s,t) tied at 8. The lesson's implementation breaks ties by sorting on the pair itself, so two runs over the same corpus produce the same table. After enough steps "west" exists as one symbol.

### The three facts the loop encodes

1. Frequency weighting makes the pairs of common words win early.
2. A pre-split on whitespace and punctuation keeps merges inside a word. A word-end marker also keeps "low" as a whole word distinct from "low" as the start of "lower".
3. The merge list is ordered. Encoding applies merges in training order, so the order is part of the artifact.

### Byte level

With bytes as the base, the first 256 ids are the byte values and merge k gets id 256 plus k. The cost of one step is linear in the corpus as a list of symbol sequences, and the sequences shrink as merges land, so a million words to ten thousand ids runs in seconds.

### What you ship

The merge table and the special-token table. The vocabulary of byte strings can be rebuilt from them.
questions.followups:
- **Level 1:** Why weight pairs by word frequency instead of counting each distinct word once? Expected: the merges should serve the text the model will see, and common words appear many times.
- **Level 2:** Why must a tie in pair counts be broken deterministically? Expected: two training runs on the same corpus must produce the same table, or the same text would get different ids.
- **Level 2:** What happens to the encoded length of a sentence as the target vocabulary grows from 300 to 600? Expected: it falls, because more merges cover longer pieces; that curve is the compression curve.
- **Level 3:** Why split the corpus into words before you count pairs? Expected: without it, merges cross word boundaries and the vocabulary fills with whole phrases that do not generalize.
questions.wrong:
- "BPE picks the pair that makes the most meaningful piece." It picks the most frequent pair; meaning is a side effect, and the likelihood-based variant is a different algorithm.
- "The vocabulary is the artifact; the merge list can be discarded." Encoding needs the merges in order; the vocabulary alone does not say how to split new text.
- "All merges are chosen at once from the initial pair counts." Each merge changes the counts, so the loop recounts after every step.

questions.title: Three ways to build a subword vocabulary
questions.prompt: Three subword algorithms dominate: byte-pair encoding, WordPiece and Unigram. Contrast how each builds its vocabulary, tell me which one can give two different segmentations of the same word on purpose, and name the libraries you would reach for.
questions.short: Byte-pair encoding merges the most frequent adjacent pair, bottom up. WordPiece also merges bottom up but scores a pair by the count of the merged piece over the product of the counts of its parts, so it prefers pairs that co-occur more than chance, and it marks continuation pieces with a double-hash prefix. Unigram works top down: it starts from a large candidate set, assigns each piece a probability, and prunes the pieces whose removal hurts the corpus likelihood least, which is why it can also sample alternative segmentations for regularization.
questions.full:
### The criteria side by side

```text
BPE merge criterion:        count(A, B)
WordPiece merge criterion:  count(AB) / (count(A) * count(B))
Unigram:                    prune the piece whose removal least lowers the corpus log-likelihood
```

The first asks which pair appears most. The second asks which pair appears together more often than you would expect from its parts. The third asks which pieces the corpus can best do without.

### Who uses what

| Algorithm | Direction | Marker | Used by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Byte-pair encoding | merge up | leading space kept on word-initial pieces | most decoder families, with vocabularies of 50,257, 128,256 and more |
| WordPiece | merge up by likelihood ratio | `##` for continuation pieces | the classic encoder with 30,522 tokens |
| Unigram | prune down | `▁` for a space when trained without pre-tokenization | an encoder-decoder family with 32,000 tokens |

### Sampling segmentations

A Unigram model is probabilistic at inference. It can return the most likely segmentation or sample another one, which gives subword regularization during training: the same word arrives in several forms and the model learns pieces more robustly. The merge-based algorithms are deterministic.

### Libraries

One library trains vocabularies for either the merge or the prune algorithm directly on raw text, encoding the space as a visible symbol and needing no pre-tokenization, which is why it is the default for multilingual work. A second, Rust-backed encoder is fast and matches the vocabularies of a widely used API family, but it only encodes. A third library trains and serves both algorithms in one place.

### Picking

Training a monolingual model: byte-pair encoding. Training multilingual: Unigram with a character coverage near 0.9995. Serving against an existing API vocabulary: the encoder-only library. Edge inference with a small model: Unigram with a smaller vocabulary.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** What is subword regularization? Expected: training on sampled segmentations from a Unigram model so the same word appears in several forms.
- **Level 2:** What does the visible-space symbol buy? Expected: the space becomes an ordinary symbol, so the tokenizer needs no pre-tokenization and works for scripts without spaces.
- **Level 3:** Which algorithm and setting for a multilingual vocabulary? Expected: Unigram trained on raw text with character coverage near 0.9995, so rare scripts are kept rather than mapped to unknown.
- **Level 3:** Why can an encode-only library not train your tokenizer? Expected: it ships pre-built vocabularies and a fast encoder; the training step lives in the other two libraries.
questions.wrong:
- "WordPiece and byte-pair encoding give the same vocabulary on the same corpus." The criteria differ, so the merges differ; the likelihood ratio favors surprising pairs over merely frequent ones.
- "Unigram is deterministic like the merge algorithms." It is probabilistic and can sample segmentations on purpose.
- "The library that encodes the space as a symbol is itself an algorithm." It is a library that trains either the merge or the prune algorithm on raw text.

questions.title: The notebook works and the service never stops talking
questions.prompt: A fine-tuned chat model answers well in the training notebook. The deployed service, with identical weights, returns rambling text that runs until the token limit. Where do you look first, and what do you expect to find?
questions.short: At the flat token sequence the model actually receives, not at the list of messages. A chat model was trained on one exact layout of role markers, special tokens and newlines; a missing newline, a swapped marker or an extra space puts the input outside the training distribution, and the end-of-turn token stops being predicted. Print the token ids of the same request from both paths and diff them, and check that the special tokens arrived as their reserved ids and not as the bytes that spell them.
questions.full:
### The model never sees the JSON

The service holds a list of role and content pairs. The model sees one flat sequence built by the chat template, which inserts markers such as a begin-of-text token, a header for each role and an end-of-turn token after each message, with specific newlines between them. Every model family lays this out differently. The template is part of the model, in the same way the vocabulary is.

### The three ways it breaks

1. **A different template.** The service used a generic layout or an older version. Each message now sits in a frame the model never saw, and the end-of-turn marker it learned is absent or misplaced, so it never predicts the stop token.
2. **Special tokens spelled out.** Special tokens must be matched exactly before the merge loop and mapped to fixed ids. If the service built the prompt as plain text and encoded it with the allow flag off, the marker string became ordinary bytes and pieces. The model sees text that looks like a marker and is not one.
3. **Stop token mismatch.** The service stops on the generic end-of-sequence id while the model emits its end-of-turn id. Generation continues past the real end.

### The check that settles it

```text
ids_notebook = tokenizer(chat_template(messages))
ids_service  = ids the service sent to the engine
diff the two lists; the first difference is the bug
```

Then decode each id back to its string and look for a marker that decoded as several pieces instead of one reserved id. If the two lists match, the input is fine and the stop token is next: compare the stop ids in the service config with the end-of-turn id that the template puts after each message.

### The fix

Use the model's own template function, pass special tokens through the reserved-id path, and configure the stop token to the id the template ends a turn with. Freeze the tokenizer file and the template together with the weights.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** What does the end-of-turn token do at inference? Expected: it is the model's signal that the answer is complete; the server must stop on that id, or generation runs to the limit.
- **Level 3:** A user types the literal string of a special token into the chat box. What should happen? Expected: with the allow flag off it becomes ordinary bytes, which is the safe default for user text; with it on, the user could inject a control marker.
- **Level 3:** How do you test a template implementation? Expected: build the sequence for a fixed message list and compare it id by id with the output of the model's own template code.
- **Level 4:** The template is correct and the ids still differ between notebook and service. What else? Expected: a different tokenizer file version, a different normalization step, or a different setting for adding special tokens at the start; hash the tokenizer file and compare the flags.
questions.wrong:
- "The sampling temperature is too high in the service." Temperature changes which token is picked, not whether the stop token is ever predicted; the ids differ before sampling.
- "The fine-tune overfit." The same weights behave in the notebook; the difference is in the input layout.
- "Trim the output on the client." That hides the symptom and the model still wastes compute on text it should not generate.

questions.title: Bake in the draft, train it after, or borrow a small model
questions.prompt: You are about to pretrain a model that will later serve a large volume using speculative decoding. Three ways to get a draft are on the table: bake sequential multi-token modules into pretraining, train a hidden-state draft head after pretraining, or reuse a small model of the same family. Give the decision with its costs, and name the gate you measure before you ship the flag.
questions.short: If I control pretraining and the hidden size is at least 4096, I bake in the sequential modules: about 10 percent slower training buys a denser supervision signal and a draft that accepts 80 percent or more at depth one. If the weights already exist, I train a post-hoc head on the verifier's features with about 60 to 200B tokens; it is backward compatible and reaches 0.88 to 0.92 acceptance on general chat. A same-family small model needs no training and sits around 0.55 to 0.70. Whatever I pick, the gate is measured acceptance on my own traffic mix at production concurrency, with the flag off below about 0.55 and the tail latency watched, not the mean.
questions.full:
### The three options

| Option | When trained | Works with existing weights | Draft parameters | Acceptance | Extra benefit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sequential modules in pretraining | during pretraining | no | one block plus a projection per depth | 0.80 and above at depth one | denser training signal |
| Post-hoc head on verifier features | after pretraining | yes | one or two layers, trained on about 60 to 200B tokens | 0.88 to 0.92 on chat | none beyond speed |
| Same-family small model | none | yes | a whole small model | 0.55 to 0.70 | none, and it costs memory |

### The decision tree

1. **Do you own pretraining?** If yes and the model is large enough, the modules are the only option that improves the model and the serving at once; the report that introduced them measured about 1.8 times generation throughput from the draft alone. At a 1B scale the overhead hurts more than it helps.
2. **Do the weights already exist?** Then the post-hoc head. It is a light training job compared with the verifier, and it does not touch the verifier's outputs.
3. **No training budget at all?** The small model, as a prototype, knowing the acceptance ceiling is low and the second model takes memory.

### The gate

Speculation is opt-in on the production engine, and the production lesson's rule is that flipping the flag without measuring acceptance on real traffic is an anti-pattern. The plan:

1. Serve the target plain and record time to first token, inter-token latency and throughput at the target concurrency.
2. Enable the draft and rerun the same benchmark.
3. Read accepted draft tokens and proposed draft tokens per request from the engine and divide the first by the second to get acceptance.
4. Below about 0.55 at production concurrency, disable the flag or train a domain-specific head.
5. Confirm that the tail inter-token latency did not get worse, because a rejected draft costs a verify and a re-roll.

### Traffic mix

A head trained on general chat sits at 0.6 to 0.8 there and falls to 0.4 to 0.6 on code, medical or legal traffic. Weight the acceptance by traffic share before you decide, and measure each slice on its own; a blended number can hide a slice where speculation is net negative. The capstone's exercise asks exactly this for a 70 percent chat and 30 percent code mix with acceptances of 0.7 and 0.4.

### Operate it

Acceptance drifts when the target changes version and the draft does not, so alert on it per slice, and keep a draft-free or n-gram fallback for the slices where the head stops paying.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** The traffic is 70 percent chat at 0.7 acceptance and 30 percent code at 0.4. How do you decide? Expected: weight by traffic share, then check each slice against the floor; code alone is below it, so route code to a plain decode or train a code head.
- **Level 4:** The target gets a new version next quarter. What happens to each option? Expected: the baked-in modules move with the model; the post-hoc head must be retrained against the new target; the small model drifts further; alert on acceptance per version.
- **Level 4:** What does a hidden-state head read in the current generation? Expected: features from several target layers, not only the last, which is part of why acceptance rose.
- **Level 4:** Where does the small-model option still win? Expected: a prototype with no training budget, or a CPU deployment where the engine ships only the plain draft path.
questions.wrong:
- "Always use the latest hidden-state draft; it is strictly best." It needs training against your target and its acceptance on domain traffic can fall to 0.4; the baked-in modules give you a draft and a better model if you own pretraining.
- "Bake the modules in later with a fine-tune." They are a pretraining choice; an existing dense model gets a post-hoc head instead.
- "Pick by the speedup on a public benchmark." Acceptance depends on your traffic; the gate is measured on your own mix at your concurrency.

questions.title: How a grammar edits the logits and why it can be faster
questions.prompt: A classifier prompt asks for one of three labels and the model answers with a paragraph, so the parser crashes. Three layers of fix exist. Explain how the strongest one works at the level of the logits, and why it is often faster than free generation, not slower.
questions.short: Prompting asks nicely, a vendor's structured-output API does it on the server, and constrained decoding does it locally by editing the logits. At each step a logit processor computes which vocabulary tokens can advance the target grammar, a JSON schema, a regex or a context-free grammar compiled to a state machine, and sets every other logit to minus infinity, so the softmax puts probability only on valid continuations and an invalid output is unreachable. It can be faster because the search space shrinks and because tokens that the grammar forces, such as a fixed key name, are emitted without a model step.
questions.full:
### The three layers

1. **Prompting.** "Return only the JSON object." The lesson puts this at about 80 percent compliance on strong models and lower on small ones. Not a contract.
2. **Native structured output.** The provider runs the constraint on its side. Reliable for supported schemas; locked to that provider.
3. **Constrained decoding.** The constraint runs in your own decoding loop and works with any local model.

### The loop

```python
def generate_constrained(model, tokenizer, prompt, fsm):
    ids = tokenizer.encode(prompt)
    state = fsm.initial_state
    while not fsm.is_accept(state):
        logits = model.next_token_logits(ids)
        valid = fsm.valid_tokens(state, tokenizer)
        logits = mask_logits(logits, valid)
        tok = sample(logits)
        ids.append(tok)
        state = fsm.transition(state, tok)
    return tokenizer.decode(ids)
```

The state machine tracks how much of the grammar is satisfied. `valid_tokens` returns the vocabulary tokens that keep the machine on an accepting path; the mask sets the rest to minus infinity. The vocabulary is about 100k tokens, so the mask is computed per state ahead of time.

### State machine or grammar engine

A regex or a flat JSON schema compiles to a finite-state machine with a constant-time lookup of valid tokens per state. Recursive schemas, nested comments or a syntax tree, need a context-free grammar engine, which handles recursion at near-zero decoding overhead in current implementations. Inference servers expose both as guided decoding.

### Why it can be faster

Fewer candidate tokens means a smaller effective search at each step. More important, long stretches of the output are fully determined by the grammar: the opening brace, a quoted key, the colon. A good implementation skips the model for those tokens and only calls it where the grammar leaves a choice.

### The library that does not touch logits

A retry-based client formats the schema into the prompt, parses the output, and retries on a validation failure, 3 times by default. It works across providers, and each retry costs latency and money. It is a different mechanism, not a weaker version of the same one.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** When does a finite-state machine not suffice? Expected: for recursive schemas; the machine flattens recursion to a fixed depth, and a context-free grammar engine is needed.
- **Level 3:** What does a provider's plain JSON mode guarantee, and what does it not? Expected: valid JSON syntax, not conformance to your schema; always send a full schema.
- **Level 3:** How does the retry library differ from the logit processor? Expected: it never changes the model's distribution; it validates after the fact and retries, which adds latency and cost per failure.
- **Level 4:** The schema has an enum with 10,000 options and compilation times out. What do you do? Expected: predict a short list of candidates with a retriever first, then constrain the decode to those.
questions.wrong:
- "Constrained decoding makes the answer correct." It makes the answer valid for the grammar; a well-formed wrong answer still passes.
- "Checking the grammar at every token makes generation slower." The valid-token sets are precomputed per state, and forced tokens skip the model, so it is often faster.
- "Enough examples in the prompt reach full compliance." The lesson's figure for prompting alone is about 80 percent; a contract needs the logits or the server.

questions.title: Design the tokenizer for a multilingual coding model
questions.prompt: You are starting a 7B model that must serve many languages and also be strong at code. Design its tokenizer: the algorithm, the library, the vocabulary size, the coverage settings, and the validation plan you would gate the training run on.
questions.short: Train a byte-fallback subword vocabulary on a corpus that mirrors the target mix of languages and code, with a pre-tokenizer that keeps leading spaces and separates digits and punctuation so that code tokenizes cleanly. For a model in the 1 to 10B range the heuristic is 50 to 100k tokens, and the multilingual requirement pushes to the top of that range or beyond it; set the character coverage near 0.9995 so that rare scripts are kept rather than mapped to unknown. Gate on tokens per word per language, the unknown rate, the compression ratio against a reference encoder and a byte-exact round trip, and freeze the tokenizer file hash in CI before the first training step.
questions.full:
### Algorithm and library

The lesson's table points to the prune-based algorithm trained on raw text for multilingual work, because it needs no language-specific pre-tokenization and handles scripts without spaces, and to the merge-based algorithm for monolingual corpora. For a mixed requirement either works if the corpus is right; the corpus mix decides more than the algorithm. Use a library that trains, not one that only encodes against someone else's vocabulary. Keep byte fallback on in either case so that no input is ever unknown.

### Vocabulary size

| Model scale | Heuristic |
|---|---|
| under 1B | about 32k |
| 1 to 10B | 50 to 100k |
| multilingual or frontier | 200k and above |

A 7B model with many scripts sits at the top of the middle row. Each added row is an embedding to learn, and the embedding matrix at 128,000 rows by 4,096 dimensions is about 524M parameters, so the size is a budget decision and not a constant. The payoff is fertility: an English-heavy vocabulary gives other scripts 2 to 3 tokens per word or worse, and non-Latin text can cost 5 to 10 times more tokens; the larger multilingual vocabulary is what repairs that.

### Coverage and code

- Character coverage near 0.9995 for a mixed corpus; refuse anything under 0.995 when rare scripts are present.
- Byte fallback for everything the coverage still misses.
- A pre-tokenizer that keeps the leading space on words, splits digit runs and punctuation, and handles whitespace runs, so that indentation and operators in code become stable pieces. Chinese characters are 3 bytes each and need merges of their own, so the corpus must contain enough of them.
- Reserve the special tokens and the chat markers at the start, with fixed ids that no merge can produce.

### The corpus

Sample the training text for the tokenizer in the proportions you want the model to be good at. A domain vocabulary can also be trained on the code corpus and merged with the base vocabulary. A tokenizer trained on an English-heavy sample will under-serve every other script for the life of the model.

### The validation plan

1. Tokens per word, per language and for code, on held-out text; this is the fertility table you publish.
2. Unknown rate, which must be zero with byte fallback.
3. Compression ratio against a reference encoder on the same held-out text.
4. Round trip, encode then decode, on all of it, including emoji and literal special-token strings. Byte-exact when the tokenizer has no normalizer; with a normalizer such as NFKC, compare against the normalized text.
5. A frozen tokenizer file hash and golden token ids in CI, so that nothing drifts between training and serving.

Flag a monolingual vocabulary under 16k as under-specified, and refuse to ship a vocabulary without the hash check.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why does the corpus mix matter more than the algorithm choice? Expected: the merges or the pruned pieces follow the frequencies in the training text, so a script that is rare in the sample gets few pieces whatever the algorithm.
- **Level 4:** What does whitespace handling do to code? Expected: indentation is runs of spaces or tabs; a pre-tokenizer that keeps whitespace runs as their own chunks lets them become stable tokens instead of being glued to the next word.
- **Level 4:** The team wants to change the vocabulary after six months of training. What do you tell them? Expected: the embeddings and every weight were trained against the current ids; a change means a retrain, which is why the tokenizer decision is gated before the first step.
- **Level 4:** How do you report the tokenizer with the model? Expected: the fertility table per language, the size and coverage of the vocabulary, the special-token list and the file hash.
questions.wrong:
- "Pick 32k because earlier models used it." That size served monolingual models under 1B; a 7B multilingual coding model pays the tax in every language.
- "Set character coverage to 1.0 to be safe." Full coverage spends vocabulary on characters seen once; near 0.9995 with byte fallback keeps rare scripts without wasting rows.
- "Train on English now and add the other languages later." The vocabulary cannot change after training without a retrain; the languages must be in the tokenizer corpus from the start.

questions.title: Why a draft that reads hidden states accepts more
questions.prompt: Walk the line from a separate small draft model to the current generation of hidden-state drafts. What limitation did each step remove, and why does feeding the draft the verifier's internal features help so much?
questions.short: A separate small model from the same family accepts around 0.6 of its tokens, because its distribution drifts from the verifier's. The first hidden-state draft replaces it with a one or two layer network that reads the verifier's last-layer features, so the draft starts from the verifier's own representation and acceptance rises to 0.7 to 0.8. The second generation proposes a tree of candidates and verifies every branch in one pass with a tree-shaped attention mask, lifting acceptance per accepted-path token above 0.85. The third drops the feature-matching loss, trains on direct token prediction, and feeds the draft its own previous outputs during training, which removes exposure bias and reaches 0.88 to 0.92.
questions.full:
### The progression

| Generation | Draft | Acceptance | Training cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Separate small model | an independently trained smaller model | 0.55 to 0.70 | none |
| Extra heads on the verifier | several output heads predicting positions ahead | 0.65 to 0.75 | about 1B supervised tokens |
| First hidden-state draft | one transformer layer on the verifier's last hidden state | 0.70 to 0.80 | about 60B tokens |
| Dynamic draft tree | the same plus a tree of candidates | 0.80 to 0.88 | about 60B tokens |
| Multi-layer features plus training-time test | fuses several verifier layers; trained on its own outputs | 0.88 to 0.92 | about 60 to 200B tokens |

### Why the hidden state helps

A separate draft re-derives from raw tokens what the verifier has already computed. The verifier's last hidden state at position t is a rich summary of the prefix, and a tiny network that reads it predicts the verifier's next token far better than a small model that reads only the token ids. The draft becomes a reader of the verifier instead of an imitation of it.

### What the tree adds

A linear chain of drafts dies at the first miss. A tree proposes several candidates at each depth, grows wider where the draft is uncertain and stays narrow where it is confident, and the verifier scores every node in one forward pass with a mask that lets each node attend only to its ancestors. The longest accepted path wins. Verification cost barely moves, because it is still one forward pass.

### What the third generation fixes

The earlier hidden-state drafts were trained to match the verifier's features, which capped how much extra data could help. The third generation trains on token prediction directly, and during training it feeds the draft its own previous predictions over several steps, the way it runs at inference. That aligns the training inputs with the inference inputs and stops error accumulation, the same fix that scheduled sampling gave sequence models. The paper reports up to 6.5 times end-to-end on chat and a 38 percent throughput gain at a batch of 64 on a production engine.

### The draft is only as good as its traffic

A general-purpose draft head trained on chat data drops to 0.4 to 0.6 acceptance on code, medical or legal traffic. A domain-specific head recovers it, and training one is a light job next to fine-tuning the verifier.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why did matching the verifier's features cap the first generations? Expected: the feature loss asks the draft to reproduce hidden states rather than predict tokens, so more training data stopped helping; the third generation trains on tokens.
- **Level 3:** What is exposure bias in this setting? Expected: the draft was trained on teacher-forced verifier inputs and run on its own outputs; the mismatch compounds over the draft steps.
- **Level 4:** What does the tree cost? Expected: a non-causal attention mask that follows the tree topology, extra stored keys and values for the tree nodes, and scheduler complexity; the verifier still runs once.
- **Level 4:** How do you compare the extra-heads design with the hidden-state draft? Expected: no second model to deploy and simpler serving, against a somewhat lower acceptance and a supervised fine-tuning stage on the verifier.
questions.wrong:
- "A larger separate draft model is the main lever." Alignment with the verifier matters more than size; a one-layer draft on hidden states beats a far larger independent model.
- "The hidden-state draft changes the verifier's output distribution to gain acceptance." The rejection rule keeps the output exact; the draft only changes how often it is right.
- "A tree needs one verifier pass per branch." All branches are verified in one pass under the tree mask.

questions.title: Why the encoder replays the merge list in order
questions.prompt: At encode time a BPE tokenizer holds the complete merge table. Why does it have to replay the merges in the order they were learned, and what goes wrong when two merges could fire at the same spot?
questions.short: Encoding must reproduce what training did to the same text, and training saw the merges one at a time in that order. If merge one created "th" and merge five created "the" from "th" plus "e", then "the" can only form after "th" exists. When two merges could apply at one position, the one with the lower rank, learned earlier, wins; change that rule and the same text yields different ids, so the model sees a distribution of ids it was never trained on.
questions.full:
### The naive encoder

```python
def encode_bpe(word, merges):
    symbols = list(word) + ["</w>"]
    for a, b in merges:
        i = 0
        while i < len(symbols) - 1:
            if symbols[i] == a and symbols[i + 1] == b:
                symbols = symbols[:i] + [a + b] + symbols[i + 2:]
            else:
                i += 1
    return symbols
```

It walks the whole table for every word, so the cost is the word length times the number of merges. Correct for a merge table trained on characters, and slow.

### The rank-based encoder

The capstone version starts from the byte split and repeats: find the applicable merge with the lowest rank anywhere in the current sequence, apply it, and scan again, until no merge in the table applies. Production encoders keep the same semantics with a rank lookup and a priority queue of candidate pairs, which runs in close to linear time.

### Why the rule is the contract

The training loop and the encoder share the merge table, and that sharing is the whole contract. Training merged the most frequent pair first, so an input that contains both halves of an early merge was always merged that way in the training data. An encoder that prefers a later merge, or the longest piece, produces a segmentation the model never saw. Nothing crashes; the ids are simply different.

### What special tokens do here

Reserved strings such as the end-of-text marker are matched exactly before the merge loop runs and mapped to fixed ids. They never take part in a merge, so no table order can split or join them.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why is the naive loop slow? Expected: it scans the full merge table for every word, so the cost grows with the table size times the word length.
- **Level 3:** How do production encoders get close to linear time? Expected: a rank lookup for each adjacent pair and a priority queue that always surfaces the lowest-ranked applicable merge.
- **Level 3:** Two tokenizers were trained on different corpora to the same vocabulary size. Do they give the same ids? Expected: no; different corpora give different merge tables and different ranks.
- **Level 3:** What test pins the order? Expected: encode a held-out word and compare with recorded ids; the capstone's tests also pin the round trip and the special-token reservation.
questions.wrong:
- "Greedily take the longest token in the vocabulary that matches." That is a different algorithm and gives a different segmentation from the training run.
- "Order does not matter because merges commute." A later merge depends on the symbols that earlier merges created, so they do not commute.
- "Sort the merges by token length." Length is not rank; a long piece may have been learned early and a short one late.

questions.title: Which multi-token design gives a free draft
questions.prompt: A pretraining team wants to supervise each position on more than the next token. One design puts several independent output heads on the backbone. Another chains small modules, one per extra depth. Which design gives you a usable speculative draft at inference, and what does it cost during training?
questions.short: The chained design. Module k takes the previous depth's hidden state and the embedding of the actual next token, runs its own small transformer block, and reuses the shared embedding and the shared output head, so its prediction of the token at t plus k plus 1 is conditioned on the token at t plus k, which is the same causal chain a decoder follows and lets the module draft tokens at inference with acceptance at depth one of 80 percent or more for about 1.8 times throughput. Independent heads all read the same hidden state and cannot condition on each other. The training cost is about 10 percent slower pretraining and about 14 h squared parameters per module, with a loss weight of 0.3 early and 0.1 later.
questions.full:
### The sequential recipe

For a prefix through position i, depth zero is the main backbone, and depth k builds on depth k minus 1:

```text
h_i^(k) = T_k( M_k · concat( RMSNorm(h_i^(k-1)), RMSNorm(E(t_{i+k})) ) )
logits_{i+k+1} = Out( h_i^(k) )
L_k = cross-entropy( logits_{i+k+1}, t_{i+k+1} )
L_MTP = (lambda / D) · sum over k of L_k
```

`E` is the embedding table and `Out` is the output head, both shared with the main model. `M_k` folds the previous hidden state and the next token's embedding into one vector. `T_k` is one transformer block. The total loss is the main next-token loss plus `L_MTP`, with lambda at 0.3 for the first 10 percent of training and 0.1 afterward.

### Why the chain matters

To predict two tokens ahead, module one sees what the next token actually was. At inference you feed it the drafted token instead, and it predicts the one after. That is exactly how a hidden-state draft works, so the trained module is a draft network for free. Parallel heads fire from one hidden state, so head two cannot use head one's answer. A verifier can still check their guesses, but they are accepted less often.

### The accounting

Per module: the projection is `2 h^2`, the block is about `12 h^2` for attention and a gated MLP, so about `14 h^2`. At a hidden size of 7168 and one module that is about 720M on paper; the published figure is 14B on a 671B main model, about 2 percent, because the module's MLP inherits the expert structure of the main model. The embedding and head add nothing, because they are shared.

### What you get

1. A denser training signal: every hidden state is supervised on D plus 1 targets, and the report shows consistent gains on reasoning, math and code evaluations.
2. A draft at inference with 80 percent or more acceptance at depth one, for about 1.8 times generation throughput, and the training-time cost is paid back the first time the model serves.

### Against a post-hoc draft

| | Post-hoc hidden-state draft | Baked-in modules |
|---|---|---|
| When trained | after pretraining | during pretraining |
| Works with existing weights | yes | no, retrain |
| Draft parameters | one or two layers | one block plus a projection |
| Acceptance | 0.88 to 0.92 | 0.80 and above at depth one |
| Benefit beyond speed | none | denser training signal |

Use the baked-in design when you control pretraining and the hidden size is at least 4096; at a 1B scale the overhead hurts more than it helps. Use the post-hoc draft when the weights already exist.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why share the embedding and the output head with the main model? Expected: no extra parameters, and the module predicts in the same vocabulary space as the backbone.
- **Level 3:** Why is the published parameter overhead larger than the `14 h^2` estimate? Expected: the module's MLP has the same expert structure as the main model, which multiplies its parameters.
- **Level 4:** With two modules, what does the second one take as input? Expected: the first module's hidden state and the embedding of the token two ahead, to predict the token three ahead.
- **Level 4:** A team wants to add this to an existing dense model by fine-tuning a new head. Your answer? Expected: the module is not trained and the backbone was not shaped by the extra loss; the lesson's position is that it needs a pretraining run, and a post-hoc draft is the right tool for existing weights.
questions.wrong:
- "The extra loss replaces next-token prediction." It is added to the main loss with a small weight; the main objective stays.
- "The module can be bolted onto a trained model with a quick fine-tune." The design is a pretraining choice; existing weights get a post-hoc draft instead.

questions.title: The same prompt costs more tokens in Korean
questions.prompt: A customer in Korea reports that the same prompt uses up far more of the context window than the English version, and the bill is higher too. Why does this happen, and what does a model builder do about it?
questions.short: The vocabulary was trained on English-heavy text, so its merges cover English and other scripts fall back to short pieces or raw bytes. Korean averages 2 to 3 tokens per word on an older vocabulary, and non-Latin text can cost 5 to 10 times more tokens than English for the same meaning; a Chinese character is 3 bytes in UTF-8, so without merges each character is several tokens. The builder's fix is a larger vocabulary trained on multilingual data, which is why one model family grew its vocabulary from 32K to 128K.
questions.full:
### Where the tokens go

A byte-level tokenizer never fails, but it only compresses what it has merges for. Each Chinese character is 3 bytes, Japanese characters are 3 to 4 bytes, an emoji is 4 bytes and can take 5 tokens. If the training corpus held little of a script, the merge table has few pieces for it, and the text stays close to one token per byte.

### What the customer feels

- The context window is a token budget, so the same document fits less often.
- Pricing is per token, so the same request costs more.
- Latency is per generated token, so answers in that script are slower.

The lesson's phrase is that a user of such a script effectively has a context window half the size of an English user's.

### What the builder does

1. Train the vocabulary on a corpus that mirrors the target language mix.
2. Grow the vocabulary so that more merges serve non-Latin scripts; the move from 32K to 128K in one family was made mainly for this.
3. Train with a library that works on raw text without pre-tokenization, so scripts without spaces segment well.
4. Measure fertility per language and report it with the model.

### How to measure it

Take the same 10 meaning-aligned sentences in English, Spanish, Chinese, Korean and Arabic, from one parallel corpus, tokenize each with the candidate vocabulary, and compare the average tokens per character. The ratios are the tax; with sentences that do not match, report them as a spot check only.
questions.followups:
- **Level 1:** Define fertility in one sentence. Expected: the average number of tokens the tokenizer produces per word, where higher means the model works harder for the same text.
- **Level 2:** How do you measure the tax for a new vocabulary? Expected: tokenize matched sentences in several languages and compare tokens per character or per word.
- **Level 2:** Why does a larger vocabulary help scripts other than English? Expected: more merges can be spent on their byte patterns, so each character or word needs fewer tokens.
- **Level 3:** What does the tax do to a product's cost model? Expected: per-token pricing and per-token latency scale with the token count, so the same feature costs more and runs slower in affected languages, and the context budget shrinks.
questions.wrong:
- "Korean is harder for the model to understand." The model sees ids; the extra cost comes from the tokenizer's merges, not from the language.
- "Use a character-level tokenizer for Korean." Characters make every sequence longer; the fix is merges that cover the script.
- "The model has a smaller context window for Korean." The window is the same number of tokens; the tokenizer spends more of them per word.

questions.title: What the split before the merges is for
questions.prompt: Before any merge runs, a production tokenizer cuts the text into chunks with a regular expression. Show me what the classic pattern does to `Hello, world! Don't stop.` and explain why the cut exists at all, given that the merges could run on the raw stream.
questions.short: The pattern cuts the sentence into eight chunks, `Hello`, `,`, ` world`, `!`, ` Don`, `'t`, ` stop` and `.`: each word after the first keeps the space in front of it, contractions split at the apostrophe, and punctuation stands alone. The merges then run inside each chunk and can never join symbols across a chunk boundary. Without the cut, training learns merges that span words, the vocabulary fills with whole phrases, and the pieces generalize worse to new text.
questions.full:
### The pattern

```text
'(?:[sdmt]|ll|ve|re)| ?\p{L}+| ?\p{N}+| ?[^\s\p{L}\p{N}]+|\s+(?!\S)|\s+
```

In order: common contraction endings, a word with an optional leading space, a run of digits with an optional leading space, a run of punctuation, and whitespace. The `\p{L}` and `\p{N}` classes need the third-party `regex` module; the standard library falls back to ASCII classes, which is wrong for multilingual text.

### Why the leading space travels with the word

` hello` and `hello` are different tokens. Keeping the space on the word means a word-initial piece and a word-internal piece stay distinct, and the decoder can rebuild the spacing from the tokens alone. The same reason forces every caller to be explicit about whether a prefix space is added at the start of a prompt.

### Why cut at all

The merge loop is greedy on frequency. In a raw stream the pair "e" followed by a space followed by "t" is frequent, so the loop would happily learn a piece that ends one word and starts the next. Such pieces do not transfer: the next text has different word pairs. Cutting first keeps every merge inside a word, which is where the regularities that generalize live.

### The other design

A tokenizer that works on raw text treats the space as an ordinary symbol and lets the merge or prune algorithm find the boundaries. It needs no language rules and handles scripts without spaces, and it allows cross-word pieces, which can compress a little better and read a little worse.

### The capstone's version

A small split on whitespace and punctuation. It is enough to keep merges inside words for a small training set, and the rest of the pipeline stays the same.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why does a prompt that starts without a space tokenize differently from one that starts with a space? Expected: the space is part of the word-initial token, so the first word maps to a different id; set the prefix-space behavior explicitly.
- **Level 3:** Why does the `regex` module matter for this pattern? Expected: the Unicode letter and number classes cover scripts beyond ASCII, which the standard library's engine lacks.
- **Level 3:** What is the trade in skipping the cut and running on raw text? Expected: no language rules and good behavior for scripts without spaces, against cross-word pieces that compress slightly better and are less interpretable.
- **Level 3:** A tokenizer file is unchanged but ids differ between two machines. What in this stage can cause it? Expected: one machine fell back to the ASCII pattern because the `regex` module was missing, so the chunks differ.
questions.wrong:
- "Pre-tokenization is just splitting on spaces." The pattern also handles contractions, digits, punctuation and runs of whitespace, and it keeps the space attached to the word.
- "The cut is cosmetic; the merges would find the same pieces." Without the cut the merges cross word boundaries and the vocabulary fills with phrases.
- "Attach punctuation to the word it follows." Then `world!` and `world` are different pieces, and the vocabulary pays for every punctuation variant.

questions.title: Two decoders, one breaks on an emoji
questions.short: Join all the bytes first and decode once, which is what `decode_a` does. A multi-byte character such as an emoji, 4 bytes in UTF-8, can be split across two or more tokens, so decoding each token's bytes alone hits an incomplete sequence and raises or emits replacement characters. The join works because every id is either one of the 256 raw bytes or the concatenation of two earlier ids, so expanding ids to bytes always ends in raw bytes, and the full byte string is valid UTF-8 whenever the input was. The `replace` option keeps the decoder from raising when a model emits a partial character at the end of a stream.
questions.full:
### Why the split happens

A byte-level vocabulary starts from single bytes and learns merges from the corpus. An emoji that was rare in training may have no merge covering all 4 of its bytes, so the encoder leaves it as two tokens, perhaps 3 bytes and 1 byte. Each token on its own is not valid UTF-8. The characters of a script with 3-byte characters have the same problem whenever a merge covers part of a character.

### Why the join terminates and round-trips

The capstone states the guarantee: encode then decode returns the input bytes exactly. The decoder concatenates the byte expansion of every id in order. Because every id is a raw byte or the concatenation of two known ids, the recursive expansion bottoms out in raw bytes, and the concatenation of all tokens is the original byte string. UTF-8 decoding then recovers the text. The test suite pins the property on an unseen sentence, on a sentence with an emoji, and on a sentence that contains a literal special-token string.

### Special tokens on the way out

The capstone's decoder checks a special-token table first and appends the marker's UTF-8 bytes, then falls through to the vocabulary, and raises on an id that is in neither. That keeps a reserved id from being looked up as a merge.

### What `errors="replace"` is for

A model can stop in the middle of a character, or a stream can be cut between two tokens that share a character. Strict decoding raises; `replace` emits a replacement character and continues. In a streaming decoder the better pattern is to buffer the trailing bytes until they form a complete character, and to use `replace` only at the final flush.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why does `decode_b` pass the English tests? Expected: ASCII characters are single bytes, so no token ever holds a partial character and every piece decodes on its own.
- **Level 3:** Design the streaming decoder in two sentences. Expected: accumulate bytes and emit only the longest prefix that is complete UTF-8, keeping the remainder; flush with replacement at the end of the stream.
- **Level 3:** Why can a word-level tokenizer not give the round-trip guarantee? Expected: unseen words map to an unknown id, and the unknown id cannot be mapped back to the original text.
- **Level 3:** What three inputs does the capstone's test suite use for the round trip? Expected: an unseen sentence, a sentence with an emoji, and a sentence containing the literal special-token string.
questions.wrong:
- "Decode each token to a string and join the strings." A token can hold part of a character, and partial UTF-8 is not a string.
- "Tell the decoder to ignore errors so nothing ever raises." Ignoring drops bytes silently and the round trip is no longer exact; the replacement character at least marks the loss.
- "The round trip only matters for the training data." Every generated answer goes through decode, and a server that raises on an emoji drops the request.

questions.title: Read one speculative step and defend each line
questions.prompt:
Read this toy speculative step from the lesson. `q_model` is the verifier and `p_model` is the draft; each returns a probability vector for the next token given a prefix.

```python
def spec_step(prefix, q_model, p_model, N, rng):
    drafts, p_probs = [], []
    ctx = list(prefix)
    for _ in range(N):
        p_dist = p_model(ctx)
        d = sample(p_dist, rng)
        drafts.append(d)
        p_probs.append(p_dist[d])
        ctx.append(d)

    q_dists = [q_model(prefix + drafts[:i]) for i in range(N + 1)]

    for i, d in enumerate(drafts):
        u = rng.random()
        if u < min(1.0, q_dists[i][d] / p_probs[i]):
            prefix = prefix + [d]
        else:
            res = residual_dist(q_dists[i], p_model(prefix))
            prefix = prefix + [sample(res, rng)]
            return prefix
    return prefix + [sample(q_dists[N], rng)]
```

Why does `q_dists` hold N plus 1 entries, what happens when the first draft token fails the test, and why does the residual use `p_model(prefix)` rather than `p_probs[i]`?
questions.short: The verifier gives a distribution at every drafted position and one more, N plus 1 in total, because when every draft is accepted the extra distribution supplies a bonus token at no extra verifier cost. At the first rejection at position i the code samples from the residual, the positive part of the verifier's distribution minus the draft's, renormalized, appends that token and returns, so every later draft is discarded. The residual needs the draft's whole distribution at that position, a vector, and `p_probs[i]` kept only the scalar probability of the token that was drafted.
questions.full:
### Why the rule is exact

Accepting a drafted token with probability `min(1, q(d) / p(d))` and otherwise sampling from `(q - p)` clamped at zero and renormalized gives samples distributed exactly as q. The theorem holds however poor p is: a bad draft rejects more often, and the output distribution does not move. That is the only reason the method is allowed in production. It is a latency optimization with no quality trade.

### Why N plus 1 verifier distributions

The verifier is queried on the prefix plus the first i drafts for i from zero to N. The first N distributions judge the drafts. The last one is the verifier's own next-token distribution after all N drafts; if everything was accepted it is free, and the step emits N plus 1 tokens from one verifier pass. In the toy the N plus 1 calls stand for a single batched forward pass over the prefix plus the drafts.

### The rejection branch

Return after the first rejection. Positions after it were drafted on a context that is now known to be wrong, so their verifier distributions are not for the sequence that is being generated. The step always produces at least one token, the residual sample, and at most N plus 1.

### The residual needs a vector

`residual_dist(q, p)` subtracts the two distributions element by element, clamps negatives to zero and renormalizes. `p_probs[i]` is one number, the draft's probability of the drafted token, enough for the acceptance test and not for the residual. The call `p_model(prefix)` recomputes the draft's full distribution at the position being corrected; in a real implementation the draft's distributions are kept from the drafting loop instead of being recomputed.

### The greedy case

At temperature zero the rule collapses to a comparison: accept if the drafted token equals the verifier's argmax, otherwise emit the argmax and stop.

### How you would test it

Run the step 10,000 times and compare the histogram of produced tokens with direct samples from q; a chi-square test passes within sampling error. Then perturb p away from q and watch the acceptance rate fall while the histogram stays put.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** `p_probs[i]` is zero and the code divides by it. Can that happen? Expected: no, the token was sampled from p so its probability is positive; the production version still guards the division and accepts when p is zero.
- **Level 3:** When does `residual_dist` divide by zero, and what should it return? Expected: when q is nowhere larger than p, which means the two are equal; return q itself.
- **Level 4:** What does the single batched verifier pass do to the verifier's stored keys and values? Expected: it extends them by N entries, and a rejection at position j must roll the logical length back to the accepted prefix plus the correction.
- **Level 4:** How many tokens does one step emit at minimum and at maximum? Expected: one, the residual sample at an immediate rejection; N plus 1 when every draft is accepted and the bonus token is sampled.
questions.wrong:
- "Accept a draft whenever the verifier gives it a probability above a threshold." A threshold changes the output distribution; the ratio test with the residual is what keeps it exact.
- "On a rejection, resample from the verifier's distribution at that position." That over-weights tokens the draft already favored; the residual removes exactly that mass.
- "Drop the bonus token to be safe." It is a sample from the verifier's own distribution and costs nothing; dropping it wastes a token per step.

questions.title: Every output validates and the answers are wrong
questions.prompt: You review the schema of an extraction service. It is `{"answer": ..., "reasoning": ..., "date": <a strict year-month-day regex>}`, enforced by constrained decoding. Compliance is perfect, yet accuracy is poor and some dates are invented. What is wrong with the design, and how do you change it?
questions.short: Two faults that no validator can catch. The answer field comes before the reasoning field, so the model commits to an answer before it has reasoned, and the strict date pattern leaves no legal way to say unknown, so the model complies by inventing a date. Put reasoning first and the answer last, and allow a null or a sentinel for a missing date; field order is logic, not formatting, and a grammar that is too strict forces a confident wrong value.
questions.full:
### Fault one: premature commitment

Generation is left to right. With `answer` first, the model must emit the label before it has written a single word of analysis; the reasoning that follows is a justification of a choice already made. Swap the order and the model writes its analysis into the context that the answer is then conditioned on. The JSON is equally valid either way. Only the second way is correct.

```json
{"reasoning": "... therefore ...", "answer": "yes"}
```

### Fault two: a grammar with no exit

The date regex admits only well-formed dates. When the source has no date, the model cannot output "unknown", and a mask that forbids every honest token leaves only dishonest ones. Allow `null` or a sentinel string in the schema and instruct the model to use it.

### The other pitfalls to check in the same review

- **Recursive schemas behind a state-machine library.** The machine flattens recursion to a fixed depth; nested structures need a context-free grammar engine.
- **Huge enums.** An enum of 10,000 options compiles slowly or times out; narrow the candidates with a retriever first, then constrain to those.
- **Plain JSON mode without a schema.** It guarantees syntax, not your fields.

### The validation plan that would have caught it

Compliance rate is one number of four. Add semantic validity, measured with a judge or a labeled set, the field coverage rate, and latency at p50 and p99. A system with perfect compliance and poor semantic validity is exactly this case.

### The rule for the team

Refuse any schema that puts `answer` or `decision` before its reasoning fields. Refuse bare JSON mode without a schema. Flag any recursive schema that sits behind a state-machine-only library.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** How do you measure semantic validity when compliance is already perfect? Expected: a labeled sample scored by a judge or by rules on the content, tracked separately from schema compliance.
- **Level 3:** The output needs a tree, such as nested comments. What changes? Expected: a state-machine library flattens recursion; move to a context-free grammar engine.
- **Level 4:** The product streams the answer to the user and wants it first for latency. How do you resolve the conflict? Expected: name the trade; options are two calls, reasoning in a hidden field before a visible answer, or accepting the latency; never answer-first with the same accuracy expectation.
- **Level 4:** How would the invented dates have shown up in monitoring? Expected: a field coverage rate near 100 percent on a corpus where the date is often missing is itself the alarm; compare the rate with the base rate of the field in the source.
questions.wrong:
- "Tighten the regex so only plausible dates pass." The grammar is already the problem; a tighter one forces more invention.
- "Add a line to the prompt asking the model to be honest." The mask forbids the honest tokens; no instruction can make the model emit a token with minus infinity logit.
- "Validation passes, so the system works." Validation checks shape; it cannot see that the answer was committed before the reasoning or that a date was made up.

questions.title: Count the windows a token stream gives you
questions.short: The target is the input shifted left by one, so an example of T input ids needs T plus 1 ids, and the count is 1 plus the floor of (N minus T minus 1) over the stride, or zero when the stream is too short. Halving the stride from T to T over 2 gives about twice the examples with half of each window shared with its neighbor, and a stride of 1 multiplies the count by about T. The loader seeds a generator with the base seed plus the epoch index, so the shuffle is the same on every restart and each epoch gets a new shuffle.
questions.full:
### The shape contract

A causal language model consumes `(B, T)` input ids and `(B, T)` target ids where the target at position t is the input at t plus 1. One slice of T plus 1 ids gives both tensors from the same memory, which makes the shift mistake impossible: `window[:-1]` and `window[1:]`.

### The count

```text
examples = max(0, 1 + (N - (T + 1)) // S)
```

The last window is dropped when it cannot fill T plus 1 ids. Padding it is valid too, but it complicates the loss mask, so the lesson drops.

### Stride against redundancy

| Stride | Overlap | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| T | none | about N over T |
| T over 2 | half of each window | about twice as many |
| 1 | almost all | about T times as many |

More overlap moves the window boundaries around, so the model sees more distinct predict-next-token tasks per epoch, at the price of more compute per epoch. Most pretraining runs use a stride equal to the context length because the corpus is already larger than one epoch can cover.

### Memory

The dataset stores one copy of the id stream and computes each window's start on the fly, so the memory cost does not grow with the number of examples the stride creates.

### Determinism

```python
generator = torch.Generator()
generator.manual_seed(base_seed + epoch)
```

The same base seed gives the same order in every epoch of every run, and the epoch index gives each epoch a new shuffle. Without this, two runs that differ in one hyperparameter also differ in data order, and the loss curves diverge for reasons unrelated to the change.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why not pad the last window instead of dropping it? Expected: padding needs a loss mask so the pad positions do not count; dropping keeps the loss simple.
- **Level 3:** Why seed per epoch and not once per run? Expected: a generator seeded once and advanced across epochs is also reproducible, but epoch k's order then depends on replaying every earlier epoch; seeding with the base seed plus the epoch index builds epoch k's order directly, which a resumed run needs.
- **Level 3:** What does a stride of 1 cost and buy? Expected: about T times the compute per epoch and heavy redundancy, against maximum boundary diversity.
- **Level 4:** You split the id stream into train and validation after windowing. What goes wrong? Expected: overlapping windows straddle the split, so validation text appears in training; split the stream first, then window each part.
questions.wrong:
- "The number of examples is N divided by T." That ignores the extra id per window and the stride; the formula has both.
- "A fixed seed makes every epoch see the same order." The epoch index is added to the seed, so each epoch gets a new shuffle and each run is reproducible.
- "The target is the same window as the input." It is the window shifted left by one; the same ids give both tensors from one slice.

questions.title: From acceptance rate to tokens per pass
questions.prompt: A draft is accepted 80 percent of the time per token and proposes four tokens per step. How many tokens does one pass of the big model produce on average, how does the draft's own cost enter, and when does a longer draft stop paying?
questions.short: The expected tokens per verifier pass are `(1 - alpha^(K + 1)) / (1 - alpha)`; at an acceptance of 0.8 and K of 4 that is 3.36, so about 3.36 times fewer big-model calls. The wall time per token is `(K c + 1)` over that expectation, where c is the draft's cost relative to the verifier, so a longer draft adds cost linearly while the geometric series saturates; at 0.8 acceptance and c of 0.05 the optimum sits around 5 to 7 drafts for about 3.2 times. The lever that matters is the acceptance rate: at a fixed K, a rise from 0.6 to 0.9 about doubles the expected tokens per pass.
questions.full:
### The formula

Each drafted token is accepted independently with probability alpha, and the step ends on the first rejected token, so the number of accepted drafts is a truncated geometric variable. Add the bonus token on full acceptance and the expectation is

```text
E[tokens per verifier pass] = (1 - alpha^(K + 1)) / (1 - alpha)
```

| alpha | K | tokens per pass |
|---|---|---|
| 0.8 | 4 | 3.36 |

At a fixed K, a higher alpha raises every term of the series, so the expectation climbs steeply as alpha nears one.

### Where the draft's cost enters

One step costs K draft forwards plus one verifier forward, `K c + 1` in verifier units. Divide by the expected tokens and you have the time per token. For a verifier at about 30 ms and a draft at about 3 ms, five drafts plus one verify is about 45 ms per step. The step emits between one and six tokens, so divide the 45 ms by the expected tokens per pass and compare the result with 30 ms for one plain token. As K grows the numerator grows linearly and the expectation flattens toward `1 / (1 - alpha)`, so there is an optimum.

| alpha | c | best K | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.8 | 0.05 | about 5 to 7 | about 3.2 times |
| 0.95 | 0.02 | about 8 to 10 | toward 5 times |

### What moves alpha

How close the draft's distribution is to the verifier's, which is a function of how the draft was built; the sampling temperature, where greedy against greedy accepts most; and the task, where code and structured output accept more than free-form prose.

### Where the formula stops being the whole story

At high concurrency the verify pass is no longer free: the decode batch already fills the memory bandwidth, and a rejected draft costs a verify and a re-roll. The production lesson's rule is that below an acceptance of about 0.55 speculation is net negative at high concurrency, so measure alpha on real traffic before you set K.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** At an acceptance of 0.95 and a draft cost of 0.02, where is the optimum? Expected: around 8 to 10 drafts, with the speedup pushing toward 5 times.
- **Level 3:** Why does the expectation saturate as K grows? Expected: it is a geometric series; the probability that all drafts up to position K are accepted falls as alpha to the K, so late positions add almost nothing.
- **Level 4:** How does batch size change the arithmetic? Expected: the verifier's extra work per draft is no longer hidden behind idle bandwidth, so the effective cost of verification and of a rejection rises, and the break-even acceptance climbs toward 0.45 to 0.55.
- **Level 4:** What single measurement do you add to the dashboard? Expected: accepted draft tokens divided by proposed draft tokens, per traffic slice, so alpha is visible where the formula needs it.
questions.wrong:
- "The speedup equals the draft length." Only if every draft is accepted; the geometric series and the draft cost cut it well below K.
- "Doubling K doubles throughput." Beyond the optimum the extra drafts are mostly rejected and their cost is paid anyway.
- "A draft ten times cheaper gives ten times the speedup." The draft cost sets c; the acceptance rate sets the expectation, and a cheap draft that is often wrong gains little.

questions.title: Take-home, a byte-level tokenizer with tests
questions.prompt: This is a take-home we send: implement a byte-level byte-pair tokenizer with training, encoding and decoding, two reserved special tokens, and a test suite. Describe the design you would submit, the tests you would ship, and the one figure you would include in the write-up.
questions.short: Reserve ids 0 to 255 for the raw bytes and a small block above them for the end-of-text and pad markers, split the corpus on whitespace and punctuation, train by counting frequency-weighted adjacent pairs and merging the top pair with a deterministic tie-break, encode by applying the lowest-ranked merge that fits until none fits, and decode by joining the byte expansions and decoding UTF-8 once. The tests pin the byte-exact round trip on an unseen sentence, on an emoji and on a literal special-token string with the allow flag on and off, plus the merge-order property and the reserved ids. The figure is the compression curve: the encoded length of a held-out sentence as the target vocabulary grows from 300 to 600.
questions.full:
### The design

```text
ids 0..255        raw bytes
next few ids      <|endoftext|>, <|pad|>
then              one id per merge, in training order
```

- **Keep the input bytes** as they are, so that the round trip is byte-exact. Compatibility normalization maps a ligature or a fullwidth letter to its plain form and is lossy, so add it only if the write-up limits the round-trip promise to normalized text.
- **Pre-split** into words and punctuation so that merges stay inside a word; the regex pattern of the large production tokenizers is an optional extension.
- **Train**: count adjacent pairs across the split corpus weighted by word frequency, merge the top pair into the next free id, record the merge, repeat to the target size. Break ties on the pair itself so two runs give the same table.
- **Encode**: match special tokens exactly first when the allow flag is on; for ordinary text start from the bytes and repeatedly apply the lowest-ranked applicable merge.
- **Decode**: special ids map to their marker strings, every other id to its bytes; join all bytes, then decode once with replacement for a partial trailing character.

### The tests

1. Round trip on a sentence the tokenizer never saw.
2. Round trip on a sentence with an emoji, where the character's 4 bytes may span tokens.
3. Round trip on a sentence containing the literal end-of-text string, with the flag off it becomes bytes and with the flag on it becomes the reserved id.
4. Merge order: a held-out word encodes to the recorded ids, and a shuffled table does not.
5. Reserved ids never appear as merge targets and never collide with byte ids.
6. Determinism: training twice on the same corpus gives the same table.

### The figure

Train to several target sizes, encode the same held-out sentence each time, and plot the token count against the vocabulary size. The count falls as merges cover longer pieces. A second line with the compression ratio, tokens over input bytes where 0.50 means half as many tokens as bytes, shows the same thing in a unit that transfers between corpora.

### What a reviewer grades

Correctness of the round trip, determinism, clean separation of the special-token path from the merge path, the quality of the tests, and a write-up that names the bug the candidate hit. Speed is not graded: Python at this scale finishes in well under a second, and production libraries in compiled languages are 10 to 100 times faster for the same algorithm.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why do the raw bytes take ids 0 to 255 before anything else? Expected: every input can then be expressed in the vocabulary before any merge exists, so nothing is ever unknown.
- **Level 3:** The input spells out the end-of-text marker as plain text. What does the allow flag change? Expected: off, the string is ordinary bytes and pieces; on, it maps to the reserved id and is skipped by the merge loop.
- **Level 3:** Why must a tie in pair counts be broken deterministically? Expected: two runs on the same corpus must give the same table, or the same text gets different ids across machines.
- **Level 4:** Replace the simple split with the production regex pattern. What do you compare? Expected: the vocabularies and the encoded lengths on the same corpus, looking at how contractions, digits and leading spaces are handled.
questions.wrong:
- "Use Unicode code points as the base symbols." Code points number in the hundreds of thousands and leave gaps for unseen characters; bytes are 256 and complete.
- "Decode each token to a string and join the strings." A token can hold part of a multi-byte character; join the bytes first and decode once.
- "Skip the pre-split to get better compression." Merges then cross word boundaries and the vocabulary fills with phrases that do not transfer.

questions.title: Speculation flies on code and stalls on creative writing
questions.prompt: Your creative-writing product samples at a high temperature and speculative decoding gives it no speedup at all, while the same setup flies on code completion. Explain the difference, and describe what the acceptance test becomes at temperature zero.
questions.short: Acceptance depends on how often the verifier agrees with what the draft sampled. At a high temperature the target distribution is flat, the draft's samples spread across many tokens, and the acceptance ratio of verifier to draft probability falls toward one over the vocabulary size, so almost every draft is rejected and the draft's cost is paid for nothing. Code and structured output are predictable, so acceptance climbs above 0.9. At temperature zero the rule becomes a comparison: accept if the drafted token equals the verifier's most likely token, otherwise emit that token and stop.
questions.full:
### Why temperature is the lever

The acceptance test is `u < min(1, q(d) / p(d))`. When both distributions are peaked on the same token the ratio is near one and the draft is accepted. Raise the temperature and both distributions flatten: the draft now samples tokens that the verifier gives little probability, the ratios shrink, and the rejections pile up. The lesson's exercise runs the loop at a temperature of 1.5 to show the collapse, where the algorithm becomes slower than plain decoding because the draft overhead stays and the accepted tokens vanish.

### Why the task matters

| Workload | Measured speedup in the lesson |
|---|---|
| chat | 2 to 3 times |
| code generation | 3 to 5 times |
| creative writing | near zero |

Code and structured output have a highly predictable next token, so even an imperfect draft agrees with the verifier most of the time; the EAGLE-3 lesson puts acceptance above 0.9 on such output. Open-ended prose at a high temperature has many acceptable continuations, and the draft rarely picks the one the verifier would.

### The greedy case

With temperature zero both models are deterministic. The test reduces to `argmax(q) == d`: accept on a match, otherwise output `argmax(q)` and stop. The residual distribution is not needed, because the verifier's choice is a single token.

### What to do about it

- Switch speculation off per request when the temperature is high, or route such requests to a plain decode pool; the EAGLE-3 lesson lists temperature-aware switching as a tuning knob.
